problems.description: Replaces SQLite (concurrency-safe) with a JSON flat file with no locking — two concurrent writes can silently clobber each other; acceptable for a scaffold but a reliability regression vs the seed.
_read_store() calls init_db() on every read path, so each request pays a stat (and possibly mkdir) on the data file even though init_db() is already called at module level.

The measured 0.70 convention score counts violations in celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, and repositories.py — files outside this commit's 2-file diff, so those are pre-existing, not introduced here.
Measurement flags 'app.py: Classes should use PascalCase' but the diff introduces no classes — likely a false positive or pre-existing code not shown in the diff.

commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested greenfield rewrite that preserves the seed's API surface, config seam, and function names while adding real validation and atomic writes, though it trades SQLite for a concurrency-unsafe JSON store.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (hmac + hashlib + manual base64url/padding) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT; the custom path is correct in the visible parts (HMAC-SHA256, compare_digest, exp check) but adds ~23 cognitive complexity and invites subtle forgery/padding bugs that a library eliminates.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' when the env var is unset, meaning tokens are trivially forgeable in any deployment that forgets to configure it.

require_auth re-reads the whole JSON store on every request and re-scans users, and each get_*/update_task call re-reads the file again — acceptable for the existing flat-file pattern but now doubled per authenticated request.

Measured convention score is 0.70 with 9 violations, but 8 of the 9 are in files this commit does not touch (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py); the only app.py entry (Classes should use PascalCase) is not introduced here since the diff adds +0 classes — the worktree-wide score overstates this commit's own convention debt.

strengths: init_db migration backfills users/next_user_id/owner_id in place and preserves pre-existing tasks instead of discarding the store.
Owner-scoping is enforced consistently across list/get/update, preventing cross-user data access.
Passwords are hashed with werkzeug's generate_password_hash/check_password_hash and signatures compared with constant-time hmac.compare_digest.
Auth helpers are extracted as small module-level functions and a require_auth decorator, keeping route handlers thin and idiomatic for Flask.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, pattern-respecting feature that layers JWT auth and per-user task scoping onto the existing flat-file store via a careful data-preserving migration, but it introduces real debt (hand-rolled JWT with a hardcoded fallback secret, +23 cognitive complexity) and the 0.70 convention score mostly reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this commit's diff.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is invoked inline in edit_task with no error isolation; if the Redis broker (default redis://localhost:6379/0) is unreachable, the core task-completion request raises and 500s, coupling primary-feature availability to the notification infrastructure.

New module-level names in the two new files (celery_app, broker_url, result_backend in celery_config.py; logger in notification_tasks.py) are lowercase, deviating from the codebase's UPPER_CASE module-constant convention (DATABASE, JWT_SECRET, JWT_EXPIRATION_HOURS) — consistent with the convention checker flagging these files.

Notification trigger logic (transition detection + owner lookup + dispatch) lives inline in the edit_task route handler, and _get_user_by_id adds a second ad-hoc data-access helper instead of a small service/domain seam.

No worker/process wiring (e.g. celery -A celery_config worker -Q notifications) or dependency-manifest update appears in the diff, so without external startup wiring the enqueued tasks are never consumed.
Tests cover the completed-transition and no-duplicate cases but not the owner-without-email path (the _get_user_by_id()/owner.get('email') guard is untested).

strengths: Notification is correctly scoped to the status transition INTO completed (previous != completed and new == completed), preventing duplicate notifications on re-completion, and is backed by a dedicated test asserting exactly one delay() call.

Clean separation of concerns: Celery app configuration isolated in celery_config.py with a named notifications queue (task_routes) and the task kept in its own notification_tasks.py module, keeping app.py thin.
Email is validated at registration and degrades gracefully for users without an email (owner.get('email') guard), consistent with the flat-file data model.
Reuses the existing get_task/update_task functional-helper pattern and matches the repo's snake_case functions, type-hinted signatures, and docstring conventions.
Uses Celery's async .delay() dispatch rather than blocking email delivery in the request path.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, well-scoped integration that fires a Celery notification only on a genuine completion transition and cleanly isolates Celery config, though the request-path .delay() couples core API availability to the broker and the new modules' lowercase module-level names drift from the repo's UPPER_CASE constant convention (mechanical 0.70).

problems.description: New repositories.py carries a module-level constants UPPER_CASE violation; overall convention score is 0.70 with 9 violations, though several (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) are pre-existing files not touched by this commit.

init_db() now only delegates to task_repository.initialize(); the UserRepository's initialization is never invoked, so user-table migration logic is only preserved if TaskRepository.initialize() covers it — behavior-preservation of the old combined init_db() is not explicit.

Repository construction via `lambda: DATABASE` couples the repositories to the app module's DATABASE constant rather than passing an explicit path/config, slightly weakening the decoupling the refactor intends.

strengths: Extracts data access into a clean TaskRepository/UserRepository layer, decoupling Flask routes from flat-file storage details
Cognitive complexity reduced by 7 with zero new bugs, smells, or duplications (SonarQube delta all non-negative)
Null-returning getters (get_by_username, get_by_id) replace inline any() scans and index-mutating store functions, simplifying require_auth/register/login handlers
Builds the changes dict in the caller and pushes mutation into update_for_owner, keeping the notification-on-completion logic intact
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped repository-pattern refactor that simplifies routes and reduces complexity with no new defects, though it leaves the module-level naming conventions unmet in the new file and punts user-table initialization onto the task repository's initialize().

problems.description: Rate-limit isolation pokes flask-limiter private attributes (`_storage`, `_limiter`, `_storage_dead`) in the client fixture — fragile against library upgrades; prefer the `RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI=memory://` config key or `limiter.reset()`.
Cursor pagination loads and slices the full task list in Python (`list_for_owner` then `tasks[start:start+limit]`) — O(n) per page; acceptable at this scale but won't generalize to larger datasets.
Cognitive complexity +16 on the `list_tasks` handler (pagination parsing + validation + cursor resolution inline); extractable into a helper to keep the route thin.
Response contract changed from a bare list to `{data, next_cursor, total}` — a breaking shape change for any consumer; tests were updated consistently, but note it.
Rate-limit tests hardcode 100 requests, coupling to the default `100 per minute` limit; 200+ requests per test run and would break if the limit constant changed.

Convention score 0.70 with 9 violations, but all 9 (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py) are pre-existing files NOT touched by this diff; the new code itself adds no new violations.

strengths: Rate limiting keys on the JWT subject for authenticated requests and falls back to IP for anonymous ones — better than blanket IP limiting.
429 handler reuses the existing `{"error": ...}` JSON convention and sets a proper `Retry-After` header.
Pagination validates input (`limit` range, integer `cursor`) and returns 400s in the established error style rather than failing silently.
Tests updated for the new contract plus comprehensive coverage: pagination pages/edge cases, rate limiting on both protected and auth endpoints, and retry-after presence.
Rate-limit storage URI is env-configurable with MemoryStorage test isolation keeping tests hermetic.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cross-cutting session — idiomatic flask-limiter + cursor pagination with good tests and consistent error handling, fit to the existing repository/JSON-error patterns, though the test isolation pokes library internals and pagination is O(n) in-memory.

compounding_issues: S1 discarded the seed's SQLite schema and rebuilt the persistence layer as a hand-rolled JSON flat-file store; every read/write rewrites the whole file (O(n) scans in list_for_owner and cursor pagination), capping scalability and forcing manual migration logic in init_db for S2's schema additions

S2 hand-rolled JWT (HMAC-SHA256/base64url) instead of a vetted library, and shipped a hardcoded default secret ('development-secret-change-me'); the decoder also never verifies the header alg matches HS256, a security-sensitive seam that persisted through S5

S3's Celery broker and S5's Flask-Limiter both default to redis://localhost:6379/0, so the completed feature set couples async notifications and rate limiting to a Redis instance that tests must mock out (MemoryStorage) to stay hermetic
S2's migration assigns owner_id=None to pre-auth tasks, silently orphaning them ('inaccessible by design'); the migration contract had to be carried intact through the S4 repository refactor
key_decisions: S1 (greenfield): replaced the SQLite seed with a dependency-free JSON flat-file store — the foundational persistence choice everything downstream (migrations, repositories, pagination) had to respect
S2 (feature_addition): hand-built HMAC-SHA256 JWT auth with user model, per-user owner scoping, and a data-loss-free init_db migration that backfills users/owner_id on existing stores

S3 (integration): edge-triggered notification enqueue (only pending→completed transitions, guarded against duplicate enqueues) behind a Celery task with a mockable .delay seam, keeping async behavior testable without a broker

S4 (refactor): extracted a BaseRepository ABC with TaskRepository/UserRepository into repositories.py, slimming app.py ~120 lines while leaving test_app.py untouched — a behavior-preserving, discipline-demonstrating refactor

S5 (cross_cutting): derived the rate-limit key from the JWT token subject (falling back to IP) so per-user limits reuse the existing auth layer, plus cursor-based pagination that threads owner filtering and newest-first ordering through the repository
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. Test count grew 6→11→13→13→17 with every suite passing at each commit, and confidence stayed at 1.0 throughout. S1 established a clean, testable flat-file foundation; S2 added auth and owner-scoping with careful migration handling; S3 integrated async notifications cleanly behind a mockable seam; S4 was a pure structural refactor that removed duplication without touching tests (a strong signal of discipline); S5 layered rate limiting and pagination on top of the existing auth and repository abstractions rather than bolting them on. The only flat spot — S4 adding no new tests — is appropriate for a refactor. Per-session cost rose modestly (0.11→0.23 USD) as the feature surface grew, matching the scope expansion.
